input:
A representative sample of an effluent stream is a portion of the stream that carries the composition of the whole over the period the sample stands for. The composition of an effluent changes with the operations that feed the stream, and the sampling arrangement is designed around that variation.

Samples are taken at a point where the stream is well mixed and where the full flow passes, so that the portion drawn off genuinely has the composition of the stream at that moment. A point downstream of a junction or a weir, where the flow is turbulent and thoroughly blended, gives a mixed sample, whereas a point in a quiet side leg gives the composition of that leg, not of the stream.

A single sample is formed from a number of increments that are taken over the discharge period. Each increment is small and is drawn at intervals throughout the period, and the increments are then combined and mixed before the sample is analysed. In this way, the combined sample averages out the variation that any single moment would otherwise freeze into the result.

A single grab sample, by contrast, can be seriously misleading, because it presents the composition at one particular moment as though that moment stood for the whole period. A discharge that varies over the course of a shift will produce a grab result that depends largely on when the bottle happened to be filled, and two grab samples taken from the same stream can differ appreciably without there having been any change in the underlying discharge. It should be noted that no numerical limits are stated here: the limits that apply to the effluent are set out in the site's permit.
